messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Error in gpa for specimens after unbending...
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Not asking any question this time, but only updating on a solution I found.
Although readland.tps can't deal with negative values, converting the tps to csv using tpsUtil helps here. Now you can do one of two: 1. add the minimum value to all coordinates and then use 'arrayspecs', 2. skip the adding minimum value to all coordinates and just use 'arrayspecs'. In both ways the 'gpagen' gives the exact same results.
Avi

messages.subject: Covariation of shape and geography
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph-ers,

I am analyzing 3D coordinate data from a sample of primate crania each of which have associated geographic information (i.e., latitude and longitude). I would like to know if cranial shape in the sample covaries with geography and, if so, what specific aspects of shape covary with geography. I am wondering what the best approach is for tackling this analysis. My inclination is that I should use a multivariate multiple regression of the GPA-aligned coordinates on latitude and longitude, but I am not confident that this is the best solution.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks in advance,
Terry Ritzman

messages.body_plain:
Terry,

What you suggest is indeed doable. But I would consider size-adjusting the shape data (or better yet incorporating centroid size into the regression model).

More importantly for understanding the biology of these taxa, I would suggest using more proximate climatic or dietary information which you believe are the actual drivers ofcranial shape. Some such variables are often easily amd freely obtained using the original spatial coordinates.

Bryan

Dear all,

I come back here with a quick question. I'm looking at my data and, graphically, there is some thing that does not make sense to me. So here I have the p-values for the tests of (angular) difference of slopes between groups:

       1      2      3      4      5      6      7

As I look at the graph I would expect to have species 1 and 6 to present a large amount of significant differences given that they look like they have a completely difference slope compared to the remaining ones. However, none of these species presents any significant difference of slope angle. In fact, as you can see, low p-values are present for species with very slight differences.

Am I doing the correct interpretation? Should I not expect to have significant differences for species 1 and 6 instead of the others?

On Tuesday, 27 March 2018 14:01:34 UTC+2, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Sergio,
> >
> >
> > For instance, with my data they retreave different results. I don't completely understand what is the difference between f1=shape ~ log(cs)+gp, f2=~log(cs)*gp and f1=shape ~ log(cs), f2=~log(cs)*gp.
>
> The former has a null model with different intercepts for groups and tests only the interaction, which is homogeneity of slopes test.  The latter forces all groups to have the same intercept in the null model (no groups at all) and tests the variation associated with different group slopes AND intercepts.  This is not a homogeneity of slopes test.  It is a test to compare a global allometry to individual group allometries.  A homogeneity of slopes test normally allows for different intercepts.  A subtle but distinctly different set of tests.
>
> Arguments could be made for doing either, but the point is that if the variation is significant, one should not look for ways to remove allometric variation but instead focus on WHY the variation is significant, which you did with your pairwise arguments (groups and slope).
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Removing the effects of size
messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

Two (maybe three) observations.

First, only group 3 looks to be qualitatively much different than the others.  I see no slope for this group compared to the arbitrarily positive slopes of the others.  (Keep in mind there is no positive or negative, other than the arbitrary assignment of such for PC 1).  As this group has such a small sample size, I would not give this difference much credit.

Second, these are fitted values and do not show the dispersion of individual values around the lines.  One of the other plotting options might give you a sense of the goodness of fit for each line.  Groups 6 and 7 might be quite variable, so although the lines look to have different slopes, the fits might not be that good, and there is a high probability fo finding greater differences by chance sampling.  Also, the ANOVA table gives you a Z-score (I am assuming small) and Rsq value (also assuming small) which might indicate that although you have “significant” group slope differences, the effect size is not that large.  Remember that P-values are not the whole story.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Removing the effects of size
messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

 I know that Mike and Dean have recently updated how they estimate the effect size (Z score) in geomorph, so I am not in a position to speak to that (Mike what should I read to understand how it has been updated?). However, I would say that given that coefficient of determination for the interaction term is on the order of 1.5%, I would suggest re-examining the angles (and associated p-values) between the allometry vectors. If the angles (vector correlations) are close to zero  (one), and p-values also not close to your alpha, you probably can make an argument for a shared allometry with several important caveats:

1) That your sample sizes within each group (your gp variable) are reasonable for estimating the allometric relationship between shape and size.
2) That you have captured a substantial amount of the variation within each group for size.

If both of these are "true" then you probably have a reasonable amount of uncertainty associated with your estimates of the allometric vector and can proceed. However, if either the within group sample size is small and/or the amount of size variation is small, then the magnitude of the allometry vector may be small (a short vector), which usually results in a poorly estimated direction of allometric effects. I am curious, what is the coefficient of determination (R^2) for the model with just shape ~ csize + gp ?

Cheers
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

Ian emphasizes an important point that echoes Mike’s response. The pairwise comparisons are of more importance here, not the overall test of the interaction term.  If you examine the matrix of pairwise effect sizes, most of these are quite small, and their corresponding significance levels are not significant. That tells you that the evidence for differences in slopes is generally quite weak (in this case, it may be driven by one or 2 pairwise comparisons: see your pairwise matrices). From my perspective that provides stronger information regarding the type of biological signal in your data and where it resides.

Ian, regarding effect size calculations, a major difference occurred starting in geomorph 3.0.5. Now we obtain effect sizes as:  observed – mean(permutation)  / std error.   This adjustment was made because we found that some statistics could vary size sample size and variable number, and so basing the effect size on the expected value from the permutation distribution was the more robust approach (see Adams and Collyer 2016: Evol.). This differs from the previous implementation which was based on Collyer et al. 2015 (Heredity) where the expected value was treated as a constant that did not vary with these components in the data (see passage in help file for procD.lm as well as above papers).

Dean

Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Removing the effects of size

Sergio,

 I know that Mike and Dean have recently updated how they estimate the effect size (Z score) in geomorph, so I am not in a position to speak to that (Mike what should I read to understand how it has been updated?). However, I would say that given that coefficient of determination for the interaction term is on the order of 1.5%, I would suggest re-examining the angles (and associated p-values) between the allometry vectors. If the angles (vector correlations) are close to zero  (one), and p-values also not close to your alpha, you probably can make an argument for a shared allometry with several important caveats:

1) That your sample sizes within each group (your gp variable) are reasonable for estimating the allometric relationship between shape and size.

2) That you have captured a substantial amount of the variation within each group for size.

If both of these are "true" then you probably have a reasonable amount of uncertainty associated with your estimates of the allometric vector and can proceed. However, if either the within group sample size is small and/or the amount of size variation is small, then the magnitude of the allometry vector may be small (a short vector), which usually results in a poorly estimated direction of allometric effects. I am curious, what is the coefficient of determination (R^2) for the model with just shape ~ csize + gp ?

Cheers

Ian

>  I know that Mike and Dean have recently updated how they estimate the effect size (Z score) in geomorph, so I am not in a position to speak to that (Mike what should I read to understand how it has been updated?). However, I would say that given that coefficient of determination for the interaction term is on the order of 1.5%, I would suggest re-examining the angles (and associated p-values) between the allometry vectors. If the angles (vector correlations) are close to zero  (one), and p-values also not close to your alpha, you probably can make an argument for a shared allometry with several important caveats:
>
>
>
> 1) That your sample sizes within each group (your gp variable) are reasonable for estimating the allometric relationship between shape and size.
>
> 2) That you have captured a substantial amount of the variation within each group for size.
>
>
>
> If both of these are "true" then you probably have a reasonable amount of uncertainty associated with your estimates of the allometric vector and can proceed. However, if either the within group sample size is small and/or the amount of size variation is small, then the magnitude of the allometry vector may be small (a short vector), which usually results in a poorly estimated direction of allometric effects. I am curious, what is the coefficient of determination (R^2) for the model with just shape ~ csize + gp ?
>
>
>
> Cheers
>
> Ian

messages.subject: Interlandmark Distances
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm pretty new to using this package (and R in general) so just wanted some help interpreting some results i got.

I'm looking at the ontogenetic changes in skull size/shape of a particular snake species (Dugite) and i wanted to calculate some linear distances between certain landmark points on the bones of my skulls. My specimens were all scanned using a Skyscan Micro-CT at the same scanning resolution (17.78um). I then processed the scan data through NRecon, then CT-Analyser to obtain the 3D models which i applied the 3D landmarks to.

I used the interlmkdist function to produce the matrix of linear distances, with the following code:

lmks <- data.frame(HL = c(1,2), HW = c(3,4), JL = c(5,6), DQL = c(7,8), MQL = c(9,10), VQL = c(12,14), row.names = c("start", "end"))
A <- dugites
lineardists <- interlmkdist(A, lmks)

##where A is the 3D array containing the landmark coordinates and lmks is the matrix of landmark addresses for the start and end landmarks defining m linear measurements

Other than this i have not done anything else with the landmark data since importing it into R. And these are the results i got below.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-2MqJp0z0lS4/WvlRn0MdbUI/AAAAAAAAAQA/Mz8PbTVdvUIGV15rzOJOumaO0KNuXbVqwCLcBGAs/s1600/Screenshot%2B%2528322%2529.png>

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Zl-U0BOdMIw/WvlRungoeRI/AAAAAAAAAQE/hDletFMmIrEXwiw2RcfyrpyZ1kCWoKvdgCLcBGAs/s1600/Screenshot%2B%2528323%2529.png>

I'm finding it hard to interpret these linear distances as i do not know what units these values are in or how to convert them to a unit useful to me. And also the measurements themselves are inconsistent as the value for the head length for a small specimen is larger than the head length of a much larger specimen.

The issue most likely stems from the fact that i haven't given R any information regarding scale or relative size. So i am just wondering how i go about calibrating these measurements. Should i obtain a reference measurement consistent across all specimens and somehow import that information into R so then it can use that to produce more accurate/useful measurements?

I apologise if i haven't explained this well enough, but as i meantioned above, I am quite the novice R user.

Any help someone can provide on this issue would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
Matt

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Interlandmark Distances
messages.body_plain:
Matt,

The units are the units you use, if you set scale during digitizing.  A distance is the square root of the summed squared distances of the partial coordinates, e.g., x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, …  This puts the distance units in whatever scale you measured, e.g., mm, m, km.  If you did not have a scale, then the units are pixels (2d photos) or whatever field increments that scanner uses.  Check your CT-Analyzer.  It must have a scale feature that allows you to turn those values into something tangible.

Regardless, distances have to be consistent with the Cartesian coordinates in the field of measurement, which has to have some kind of scale.  Often we wish to convert one scale to another (like pixels to mm), but to do that, one needs to know the initial scale.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject_clean: ProcD.pgls of shape against multivariate diet with a factor
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to understand the strength of the association between bird beak shape and diet in my data. My beak shape data is Procrustes residuals and diet data is PCoA (Principal Coordinates Analysis) scores from non-continuous dietary data from an online dataset.

I will generally use Partial Least Squares to understand the strength of this association but I wanted to include a behavioural factor in the analysis and I do not think that’s possible with PLS (or is it?).

Anyway, I am trying to use procD.pgls function with the following and I getting this error:

beak_data <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = beak_coords2, diet = diet2, MA = as.numeric(ant.MA1), BM = as.numeric(log.BM1), UBF.C = as.factor(UBF1), phy = birdTree.pruned)

PGLS.coords_diet <- procD.pgls(coords ~ diet*UBF, data = beak_data, phy = phy, iter = 999)

Error in model.frame.default(object, data, xlev = xlev) :

  invalid type (list) for variable 'diet'

both ‘beak_data$coords’ and ‘beak_data$diet’ are matrices with taxa as row names,

An alternative I read before in this forum before is convert into numeric variables each of the Principal coordinates (i.e. PCo1, PCo2, etc) and include each in the linear model but this will only give me the association between shape to each of the individual PCos, won’t it?

Is there any way around this?

Thank you very much,

Guillermo

messages.body_plain:
Guille,

Your error suggests that your variable is not formatted correctly.  It appears it is a list rather than a vector.

This commonly happens when a vector is part of a list and the only component in the list.

You can try to diagnose this two way.  First,

class(diet)

if it returns, “list”, then you should change the class.  Second, try this

diet[[1]]

If more than one value is returned and it looks like the factor you expect, then it means the factor occupies the who first part of a list.  In theses cases,

diet <- diet[[1]]

usually fixes things.

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
The error occurs while attempting to make a model frame - not a geomorph function, but one called by the geomorph function - so the issue might be with your data frame you are using, beak_data.  Is $diet a matrix in your data frame?  A problem could be that the 10 variables are in the data frame but not as a matrix.

Try attributes(beak_data) or beal_data$diet to confirm.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much Ian, Michail and Dean. I was a bit lost because graphically I could not detect slope heterogeneity.
I'm more sure now of how I should interpret my results.

Cheers

On Friday, 11 May 2018 19:51:40 UTC+2, Ian Dworkin wrote:

> Dean,
>
> Thanks so much, that explains it, and may I say, a very neat idea. I definitely have to think about it further (I will re-read the 2016 paper in Evolution). Thanks so much.
>
> Ian

> On 11 May 2018 at 13:30, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> > Sergio,
> >
> >
> >
> > Ian emphasizes an important point that echoes Mike’s response. The pairwise comparisons are of more importance here, not the overall test of the interaction term.  If you examine the matrix of pairwise effect sizes, most of these are quite small, and their corresponding significance levels are not significant. That tells you that the evidence for differences in slopes is generally quite weak (in this case, it may be driven by one or 2 pairwise comparisons: see your pairwise matrices). From my perspective that provides stronger information regarding the type of biological signal in your data and where it resides.
> >
> >
> >
> > Ian, regarding effect size calculations, a major difference occurred starting in geomorph 3.0.5. Now we obtain effect sizes as:  observed – mean(permutation)  / std error.   This adjustment was made because we found that some statistics could vary size sample size and variable number, and so basing the effect size on the expected value from the permutation distribution was the more robust approach (see Adams and Collyer 2016: Evol.). This differs from the previous implementation which was based on Collyer et al. 2015 (Heredity) where the expected value was treated as a constant that did not vary with these components in the data (see passage in help file for procD.lm as well as above papers).
> >
> >
> >
> > Dean
> >
> >
> >
> > Dr. Dean C. Adams
> >
> > Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program
> >
> > Professor
> >
> > Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology
> >
> > Iowa State University
> >
> > www.public.iastate.edu/~dcadams/ <http://www.public.iastate.edu/~dcadams/>
> >
> > phone: 515-294-3834
> >
> >
> >
> > From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Ian Dworkin
> > Sent: Friday, May 11, 2018 12:04 PM
> > To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
> > Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Removing the effects of size

> >
> >
> > Sergio,
> >
> >
> >
> >  I know that Mike and Dean have recently updated how they estimate the effect size (Z score) in geomorph, so I am not in a position to speak to that (Mike what should I read to understand how it has been updated?). However, I would say that given that coefficient of determination for the interaction term is on the order of 1.5%, I would suggest re-examining the angles (and associated p-values) between the allometry vectors. If the angles (vector correlations) are close to zero  (one), and p-values also not close to your alpha, you probably can make an argument for a shared allometry with several important caveats:
> >
> >
> >
> > 1) That your sample sizes within each group (your gp variable) are reasonable for estimating the allometric relationship between shape and size.
> >
> > 2) That you have captured a substantial amount of the variation within each group for size.
> >
> >
> >
> > If both of these are "true" then you probably have a reasonable amount of uncertainty associated with your estimates of the allometric vector and can proceed. However, if either the within group sample size is small and/or the amount of size variation is small, then the magnitude of the allometry vector may be small (a short vector), which usually results in a poorly estimated direction of allometric effects. I am curious, what is the coefficient of determination (R^2) for the model with just shape ~ csize + gp ?
> >
> >
> >
> > Cheers

> > > > > >
> > > > > > The former has a null model with different intercepts for groups and tests only the interaction, which is homogeneity of slopes test.  The latter forces all groups to have the same intercept in the null model (no groups at all) and tests the variation associated with different group slopes AND intercepts. A subtle but distinctly different set of tests.

messages.subject: Multiple levels of allometry
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I would like to see the effect that individual size (i.e. body length) has on head shape. Because size is a measure of allometry, I tried correlating centroid size (of the head) with individual size (of the whole organism)  but they do not correlate (results have F-values of 0, which suggests that there is something wrong with my model, yet plots show no correlation, i.e. points lie almost exactly on a horizontal line).

I seem to be in a position where my results are confounded due to multiple measures of allometry (as Klingenberg 2016 suggests), and I am therefore unable to disentangle variation due to allometry of the head, or individual size.

I am wondering how is now best to proceed....I tried including 'log(CSize)' as a covariate in all of my models, but this took up a lot of my variation. I have a feeling that it will be impossible to avoid this? Is it possible to proceed in hierarchical levels? I.e. removing allometry in levels that have parallel slopes, or if the null hypothesis of parallel slopes is rejected, is it possible to remove CSize from the model and just use individual size, stating that "significant results may be an artefact of allometry, but since individual size is also considered a measure of allometry we proceed using individual size only"?

Thanks in advance,
Sam

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Multiple levels of allometry
messages.body_plain:
Sam,

If you have no correlation between body length and head Csize, and the plots confirms this result, then the two measures are not confounded. thus I see no problem here that needs to be solved; nor do I see how head shape variation with body size is confounded with head Csize, as the two size measures are uncorrelated.  One can simply perform the shape ~ body length analysis to evaluate allometry with body length.

Now, if body length and head Csize were correlated, then there would be complications, as covariation trends of each size measure with shape could partially overlap in terms of the variation they each explain.  Using a combined model and type II sums-of-squares could be beneficial and provide a path forward, but more care in interpretation is still required (see Adams and Collyer 2018 Evol. for an example where type II SS aided in biological interpretation of confounding independent factors). But again, since in your case there is no strong (or apparently any) correlation between body length and head Csize, there is no such issue to worry about.

Finally, I believe there is some confusion in terminology that should be cleared up. Multiple levels of allometry typically refers to the biological levels in which allometry resides (static vs. ontogenetic vs evolutionary allometry). It does not typically refer to allometry revealed when using different size measures in the shape ~ size regression.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Multiple levels of allometry

Hi everyone,

I would like to see the effect that individual size (i.e. body length) has on head shape. Because size is a measure of allometry, I tried correlating centroid size (of the head) with individual size (of the whole organism)  but they do not correlate (results have F-values of 0, which suggests that there is something wrong with my model, yet plots show no correlation, i.e. points lie almost exactly on a horizontal line).

I seem to be in a position where my results are confounded due to multiple measures of allometry (as Klingenberg 2016 suggests), and I am therefore unable to disentangle variation due to allometry of the head, or individual size.

I am wondering how is now best to proceed....I tried including 'log(CSize)' as a covariate in all of my models, but this took up a lot of my variation. I have a feeling that it will be impossible to avoid this? Is it possible to proceed in hierarchical levels? I.e. removing allometry in levels that have parallel slopes, or if the null hypothesis of parallel slopes is rejected, is it possible to remove CSize from the model and just use individual size, stating that "significant results may be an artefact of allometry, but since individual size is also considered a measure of allometry we proceed using individual size only"?

Thanks in advance,

Sam

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] ProcD.pgls of shape against multivariate diet with a factor
messages.body_plain:
Guille,

>From what you sent, the problem likely lies upstream of any geomorph analyses. In fact, I suspect that somewhere in your data preparation pipeline you are using the geiger function ‘treedata’ to match and prune a data matrix with your phylogeny.

There is a known bug in geiger’s ‘treedata’ when the datamatrix being pruned contains columns with multiple attributes: some numeric, some as factors or characters. In these cases, ‘treedata’ automatically converts all columns to character; which needless to say is undesirable!

There are several workarounds. One is to break up your data  frame into numeric only and character/factor only first, then run them through ‘treedata’. Another is to run the entire data frame through ‘treedata’ then manually separate out the sub-parts, force them back into numeric, matrices of numeric (don’t forget the dimensions!), etc.

Then, and only then would I put these into a geomorph data frame for further analysis.

Dean

messages.subject_clean: Doubts in a simple allometry analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello
I have some experience with Elliptic Fourier analyses in R and, but I have some issues using geomorph. Sorry If this was covered in in the mail group but I couldn’t find it.

I am trying to perform a simple allometry analysis.

>coords_gpagen<-gpagen(A = coords, curves = NULL, surfaces = NULL, PrinAxes = TRUE,max.iter = NULL, ProcD = TRUE, Proj = TRUE, print.progress = TRUE)

>gdf_crudo<-geomorph.data.frame(coords_gpagen, species=mydata$Especie)
>allometry_gdf_crudo<-procD.allometry(coords~Csize,~species,data=gdf_crudo)
I get a significant p for the covariates and for the interaction
> plot(allometry_gdf_crudo, method="PredLine", gp.label = T)

> plot(allometry_gdf_crudo, method = "RegScore", gp.label = T)

Is there an easy way to plot the trajectories for other PCs besides pc1?

Is there a way to extract the slope of the regressions for each PC for each species?(the PredLine plot only shows  PC1)

>From the pca (see attachment) I notice a clear positive correlation between size and both PC1 and PC2. I understand the PCs (and slopes) signs are relative, but shouldnt the pca and PredLine signs match? (see attached graphs)

I aso tried with

>procd_gdf_crudo<-procD.lm(coords~Csize*species,data = gdf_crudo)

I get simmilar results but I can’t find the slope for each species in the results.

4)I would also like to compare the slopes but I get a silly error when I tried to do advanced.procD.lm:

>gdf_crudo<-geomorph.data.frame(coords=coords_gpagen$coords, species=mydata$Especie, Csize=coords_gpagen$Csize)

>PW<-advanced.procD.lm(f1= coords ~ Csize*species, f2= ~Csize+species, iter=999, data = gdf_crudo)

Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object 'species' not found When I called other functions with species in the formulae I had not any issue. PS: I cant find the quick guide for the 3.0 version (I am working with a cache web version but it is incomplete and poorly formatted) and also the github wiki is not working, is there any other oficial resource? Thanks in advance Santiago Morello

On Monday, May 14, 2018 at 9:45:16 PM UTC+8, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Matt,
>
> The units are the units you use, if you set scale during digitizing.  A distance is the square root of the summed squared distances of the partial coordinates, e.g., x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, …  This puts the distance units in whatever scale you measured, e.g., mm, m, km.  If you did not have a scale, then the units are pixels (2d photos) or whatever field increments that scanner uses.  Check your CT-Analyzer.  It must have a scale feature that allows you to turn those values into something tangible.
>
> Regardless, distances have to be consistent with the Cartesian coordinates in the field of measurement, which has to have some kind of scale.  Often we wish to convert one scale to another (like pixels to mm), but to do that, one needs to know the initial scale.
>
> Cheers!

> Mike
>

messages.subject: Issues with the procD.lm in the new geomorph version
messages.subject_clean: Issues with the procD.lm in the new geomorph version
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

a colleague of mine wants to do GMM. She started with exploring measurement error. Her data are quite simple at the moment containing 5 specimens with 10 LMs. Her script looks like this:

Test<-readland.tps(file.choose(),specID="imageID",readcurves=FALSE)

rep = as.factor(c(rep(1,3),rep(2,3),rep(3,3),rep(4,3),rep(5,3)))
pos = as.factor(paste("D",1:15,sep=""))

Test.list<-list(Test,rep,pos)
names(Test.list) = c("land", "rep","pos")

Test.gpa <-gpagen(Test.list$land)
shape=Test.gpa$coords

My.df<- geomorph.data.frame(shape,rep,pos)

ANOVA1 <- procD.lm(shape ~ rep/pos, iter=999, data=My.df)
ANOVA2 <- procD.lm(shape ~ rep, iter=999, data=My.df)

This worked perfectly well with her data on my computer. I still have an old version of R (version 3.3.3) and geomorph (3.0.3) on my computer [it's quite cumbersome to get a new version of R installed because the responsible person is in only once a week]. My colleague has now tried to run the exact same script on her computer with the newest versions of R and geomorph. She get's the following error meassage:

ANOVA1<- procD.lm(shape ~ rep/pos, iter=999, data=My.df)
Error in procD.fit(f1, data = data, keep.order = ko, pca = FALSE, ...) :
  Your formula appears to have data embedded within objects
(a '$' is part of the formula).  It is not possible to reconcile
the location of the data from the object that contains it with this
function.  Either use a geomorph data frame or liberate the data from
the object and try again.

We checked the geomorph dataframe My.df which does not contain any $ but is a list with three elements.

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Issues with the procD.lm in the new geomorph version
messages.body_plain:
Nadja,

First, this is a poor error statement that we introduced to try to help users understand why an error might have occurred rather receives R’s indecipherable error statement.  However, it seems to get trigger for errors for which we did not intend it.  We need to update that, but for now, read it is simple as “something went wrong”

Second, thank you for providing the detail of your analysis!  It helps to see where the error might have occured.

The problem appears that the objects in your geomorph data frame do not have names.  Try this and see if it works

 My.df <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = shape, rep.pos = rep,pos)

If you do not give them names, they are nameless at positions [[1]] and [[2]] in the list.  The function is searching for names found in the formula and cannot match them.  (This is what the error is detecting and often that is caused by subsetting a list in the formula name.)

This might seem like an unneeded redundancy but from the R perspective, variables, factors, matrices, and other data frames can be added to data.frames, so it is essential to name components.  Note that with geomoprh.data.frame, we have some exceptions, like with gpagen objects.  The function will separate the components and add them separately.  You could do this

My.df <- geomorph.data.frame(Test.gpa, rep.pos = rep,pos)

and the objects in the data frame will be $coords, $Csize, and $rep.pos

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: geomorph 3.0.6 released
messages.body_plain:
Hello geomorph users!

Version 3.0.6 of geomorph has now been released and is up on the CRAN repository for download and installation. As with all version updates, changes have been documented in the News file.

Of particular note is the incorporation of a refined residual randomization permutation procedure (RRPP) which is more general than its predecessor. For OLS models, the method is equivalent to the previous version and thus unchanged. However, for GLS models, the refined RRPP procedure is preferable and more widely applicable for statistical designs such as phylogenetic regression, phylogenetic anova, and phylogenetic factorial models.

A discussion of the procedure, and of the theory of exchangeable units from which the method is derived, is found in a recent paper in Evolution: Adams and Collyer. 2018. Phylogenetic anova: group-clade aggregation, biological challenges, and a refined permutation procedure. (found at  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/evo.13492 ). Also, for the macroevolutionary biologists in the group, that paper also discusses how group dispersion across the phylogeny can affect statistical and thus biological inferences with respect to covariation patterns with phenotypic traits.

Best,

Dean (on behalf of the geomorph team: Dean, Mike, and Antigoni)

Santiago,

Please see the help file for procD.allometry and procD.lm.  The output from those functions is far greater than just the anova table (one can extract model coefficients, permuted values, predicted values, etc.). There are also numerous examples of the use of the functions in the help files.

For plotting, there are multiple options: PredLine, RegScores, CAC, and equivalent output options from procD.lm.  Again see the help files for the plotting options of these analytical functions.

As for directionality of the plots you sent: there is no reason to believe they will coincide in direction. Both plots have some type of data rotated their principal axes, and since the positive and negative ends of such axes are arbitrary, they may not coincide. Also, note that the PC plot is PC1 vs PC2: there is no intuition that directions in this shape-only space would coincide with directions of covariation between shape and size (the second of your plots). A bit more inspection and pondering of the data and the outputs would provide some insight I think.

Best,

Dean

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Issues with the procD.lm in the new geomorph version
messages.body_plain:
Nadja,

It could be one or a combination of changes made in our updates or R updates.  I don’t recall an explicit major change to geomorph data frames but it is possible an update somewhere else created an issue here, which we also neither tried to anticipate nor override. Geomorph data frames are R lists and the way you had it set up essentially asks R to try to give objects in the list a name or give up if it is unattainable. The solution I gave you is unambiguous because you define the names.

Also, as a possibility, a change in the way our functions search the list to find data might have assumed that the list had names. I know that our old coding did not always do a good job to match names. Updated code has become more efficient. It might be that your example just happened to work better with our old code that had more bugs.

These are speculative ideas. Invariably, with program coding, fixing one issue introduces another elsewhere.  I’m surprised your example worked with our old version. I would not have expected that. We probably just got lucky because we assumed the data frame would have named objects.

Cheers!
Mike

data(plethodon)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, species = plethodon$species, site = plethodon$site)

1. coords [1:12, 1:2, 1:40]
2. Csize [1:40]
3. species: factor w/4 levels (with an equal number of values to match 1:40)
4. site: factor w/2 levels  (with an equal number of values to match 1:40)

Jeremy

Thank you for providing more detail.  Now I can pinpoint the error.  I replicated your error, and the problem is that you likely created a model design matrix with empty variables.

attr(,"assign")
[1] 0 1 1 1 2 3 3 3
attr(,"contrasts")
attr(,"contrasts")$species
[1] "contr.treatment"

attr(,"contrasts")$site
[1] "contr.treatment"

Notie the last two columns are all 0s.  This will not work in trajectory.analysis.  The error message might not be helpful to diagnose this, but it caused the same error for me that you found.

Note, if I changed the species factor above to species <- factor(rep(1:4, 10)), so that it had in order 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, …. instead of 1,1,1,1, …., 2, 2, 2, 2, …., then the design matrix was full-rank and the analysis worked.

So now my hunch is that you have a case where at least one level of one factor is not represented in the other factor.  You can create a model matrix like I did above to check that for your data.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to quantify the strength of the relationship between beak shape and diet in some birds.  As I am aiming to understand this relationship at a wide macroevolutionary scale I am using a behavioural category as a factor (UBF.C) with 5 levels to account for many-to-one and one-to-many (and many-to-many?) relationships between diet and feeding behaviour.

The behavioural groups range in size from 1 specimen (only one of them, whose values I am not going to interpret and it is probably not affecting a lot to the general model or is it?) to ~ 60 specimens and when I conducted pairwise phylogenetic Procrustes ANOVA the mean values of some are well distinguished based on beak shape:

>PGLS.coords_UBF <- advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ UBF.C, coords ~ 1, group= ~UBF.C, phy = beak_data$phy, data = beak_data, iter=999)

 Now, if I understood well my linear model should be (i.e., not including the factor UBF.C as a variable but only the interaction between both diet and UBF.C):

> PGLS.coords_diet <- procD.pgls(coords ~ diet2 + diet2:UBF.C, data = beak_data, phy = phy, iter = 999, print.progress = T)

            Df       SS         MS     Rsq      F       Z Pr(>F)

diet2        10 0.009492 0.00094919 0.16151 3.7093 0.20322  0.431

diet2:UBF.C  41 0.017804 0.00043424 0.30294 1.6970 1.45910  0.071 .

Residuals   123 0.031475 0.00025589

Total       174 0.058771

---

Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

There is not a significant relationship between beak shape and diet as quantified here and the relationship between both variables does not depend on feeding behaviour, which is congruent with earlier results.

Now when I include UBF. C as a variable in the linear model the interaction between diet and UBF. C is indeed significant (and also the degrees of freedom weirdly change)!

             Df       SS         MS      Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
diet2        10 0.009492 0.00094919 0.161507 3.6940 0.1894  0.434
UBF.C         5 0.005278 0.00105558 0.089805 4.1081 3.1728  0.002 **
diet2:UBF.C  40 0.013424 0.00033559 0.228406 1.3060 1.7822  0.035 *
Residuals   119 0.030577 0.00025695
Total       174 0.058771
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

How can they behave so differently both linear models? The ratio Residual SS : Total SS is similar in both cases but the significance changes completely.

Also, can I interpret: (1- (SS explained by significant factors/ Total SS)  =  SS explained by the model)?

I am a bit puzzled about these results and any insight would be much appreciated

Thank you in advance,

Guille

messages.body_plain:
Mike,

Okay this makes sense why there's an error - thanks for clarifying. In this case it would seem that using trajectory analysis won't work with my data as sites are nested in region.

So: trajectory.analysis(coords~region*site) would cause an error because the resulting data matrix would not be symmetrical as some term combinations do not exist.

If I run the analysis with only site, I get an error asking me to specify the number of trajectory points. So I'm going to assume at this point I am unable to use this analysis to visualize the different shape trajectories by site?

As an aside, in the description for trajectory.analysis it does seem to imply that I would be able to perform this analysis with either one term, or more as long as the order of the terms match the specimen order. Which in my case this is true. But it seems that there are some assumptions here; one being when including two discrete terms they must be balanced or be ordered. This should be mentioned if this really is the case. Obviously if none of this is relevant of course ignore.

As always thank you for your prompt and thorough responses - much appreciated!

Cheers,
Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

trajectory,analysis is a special analysis, unlike the versatile pairwise comparisons one can do in advanced.procD.lm.  If you have a nested design, it might not be the right analysis.  If however, you feel like your sites are commensurate (maybe high-latitude versus low altitude, or lake versus stream, or something along these lines), you can create a new factor from the site factor that has representation in both species factors, and the analysis should work.

The other option in trajectory.analysis is if you have data arranged as a concatenated set, e.g., | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | … | Yp |, for the p points of a trajectory, where Y are data matrices.  I don’t think this is what you want to do, if your data are not already arranged as such.

Good luck!
Mike

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Huge discrepancies between similar linear models using procD.pgls
messages.body_plain:
Guille,

A few comments.

First, from an earlier post I recall that diet is actually a matrix of PCoA coordinates. So while you have it coded as a single ‘thing’, it is really 10 different continuous covariates. Thus you are really doing Y~diet1+diet2+diet3… etc.  That is quite a large multivariate multiple PGLS regression.

Second, you have a grouping factor, so phylogenetic anova.  BEFORE proceeding, be certain to download and install geomorph 3.0.6 from CRAN.  Yesterday we announced the version and the primary advance was a more appropriate permutation test for GLS models like phylogenetic anova (the corresponding paper is in press in Evolution).

Third, the df do make sense in the full factorial. The df for an interaction in full factorial is dfA*dfB.  That is 10*4 = 40.

As for the different ‘behavior’ (by this I think you meant significance), this one requires some more thinking about linear models. You are using type I SS, so each term in the 2 is being compared to a reduced model with one fewer term. The difference in how SS is partitioned in your two models relative to those reduced models will explain it.

However, this may not be the most appropriate manner to evaluate your data if diet and UBF covary. If they do you may wish to use conditional (type II) SS.  See the example for phylogenetic MANCOVA in the evolution paper just mentioned (Adams and Collyer 2018. Evolution: early view on-line).

Dean

diet2        10 0.009492 0.00094919 0.161507 3.6940 0.1894  0.434
UBF.C         5 0.005278 0.00105558 0.089805 4.1081 3.1728  0.002 **
diet2:UBF.C  40 0.013424 0.00033559 0.228406 1.3060 1.7822  0.035 *
Residuals   119 0.030577 0.00025695
Total       174 0.058771
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

How can they behave so differently both linear models? The ratio Residual SS : Total SS is similar in both cases but the significance changes completely.

Also, can I interpret: (1- (SS explained by significant factors/ Total SS)  =  SS explained by the model)?

I am a bit puzzled about these results and any insight would be much appreciated

Thank you in advance,

Guille

If however, you feel like your sites are commensurate (maybe high-latitude versus low altitude, or lake versus stream, or something along these lines), you can create a new factor from the site factor that has representation in both species factors, and the analysis should work.
>
> The other option in trajectory.analysis is if you have data arranged as a concatenated set, e.g., | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | … | Yp |, for the p points of a trajectory, where Y are data matrices.  I don’t think this is what you want to do, if your data are not already arranged as such.

> Good luck!
> Mike

messages.subject_clean: Am I using the right approaches with this dataset?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Geomorph Community,

I have a complex dataset I'm working with and I would greatly appreciate some advice. In order to finalize my results I'd really like to know that my approach is actually appropriate to test my hypotheses. Here's a quick summary of the data that I have and my approach.

I'm investigating how size and shape affect the tuning of ears in an insect. semilandmarks with curves were placed on 3D volumes of the hearing system of 48 individual animals. The 48 individuals are from 8 different populations (6/population) with uneven numbers of genders in each population. Although I'm not as concerned about differences in gender here. Also, the 8 populations separate out (nested) into a northern (4 populations) and southern region (4 populations). My hypotheses are: 1) Both size and shape affect tuning of the ear. 2) Shape (& size) differs by region and by population. I also have three different body size measurements: centroid size, prothorax width, and weight.

My current approach:
Investigation of size variables - e.g. distributions (weight needed to be log transformed as it differs significantly from a normal distribution), ANOVA (by gender (NS), region (highly significant for all three size variables) and by population (highly significant: post-hoc tests reveals 4 size classes for each size variable)), correlation matrix (all three size variables highly correlated)
GPA of two sets of placed landmarks (to test for user error in placement)
Test of user error <- proc.D.lm(coords ~ group) group contains set 1 and set 2 of placed landmarks - NS
I am taking forward one set of the above GPA aligned coordinates in the below analyses
Shape differs by population?
advanced.procD.lm(coords~pop, ~1, groups = ~pop) - Highly significant with several significant pairwise comparisons
Shape differs by region?
advanced.procD.lm(coords~region, ~1, groups = ~ region) - significant but both f and z scores are low (2.23/2.1)
Shape differs by gender?
advanced.procD.lm(coords~gender, ~1, groups = ~gender) - NS
Investigation of allometry without data structure
Centroid size <- procD.lm(coords~Csize) - NS
Prothorax width <- procD.lm(coords~prow) - Right at significance 0.05
log(weight) <- procD.lm(coords~weight) - significant
Investigation of allometry with data structure
Are there differences in shape by population when accounting for body size?
advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~Csize + prow + log(weight) + region * pop, groups = ~region*pop) - significant model with a few significant pairwise comparisons
Are there differences in shape by population when accounting for separated out body size variables (this was done in order to get a better idea of how they interact with data structure alone)
Centroid size <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~Csize + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with several significant pairwise comparisons
Prothorax width <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~prow + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with a couple significant pairwise comparisons
weight <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~log(weight) + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with several significant pairwise comparisons
PCA reduced allometric shape and PCA reduced allometry free shape (from applying the residuals from the analyses in #7 on GPA consensus coordinates).
PCA reduced shape is used in multivariate multiple linear regression analyses to address hypotheses 1.
Does my above approach to address my second hypothesis seem reasonable? At present, these results support the conclusion that shape does differ by population, region and by size. Although pairwise comparisons suggest that not all populations differ significantly from each other (when accounting for all body size measurements or with them individually).

Any insights and constructive comments are very welcomed and appreciated. As I've said, I am very interested in finalizing these results.

Thank you in advance for your time - cheers,
Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Andrew, readland.tps is intended for reading landmark coordinates BEFORE superimposition. Because you have performed GPA in tpsRelW, you have negative numbers which are read into geomorph as NAs and appear as missing data. I suggest you try reading in your data before superimposition and then use gpagen to perform GPA inside geomorph, or you find some way other than readland.tps to read in your superimposed data.

Good luck!

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

A few quick thoughts. First, if all variables are considered main effects, one should consider a factorial analysis in procD.lm: Y~pop + region + pop:region.  However, I suspect that your populations are nested within region, so a nested model is preferred. The help file of both procD.lm, advanced.procD.lm, and nested.update have more details on how to run this.

Second you mentioned allometry. This too could be a factor in the model. That is actually important, because patterns of allometry may differ among factor levels; converting your problem to an ancova.

Finally, at the end you mentioned running an analysis, reducing the data dimensions and running subsequent analyses on the reduced data. That is never a good idea: the algebra does not care about the dimensionality (at least as run in geomorph and the RRPP package). Take advantage of it and run it fully (note: reducing data one can both introduce patterns or miss patterns in the first few PC dimensions, as covariation of Y with X is not guaranteed to be in the first few PC dimensions of Y).

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Dean,

Thank you very much for your time, thoughtful comments and feedback. Actually my original approach included using procD.lm instead of advanced.procD.lm in order to look at factor interactions. But based on other conversations, I was persuaded to switch to advanced.procD.lm. Fortunately, whether I'm suing procD or advanced, all of the same trends appear from this dataset - so that's a plus. I will revisit using procD.lm incorporating nested.update for the factors.

Yes, allometry does seem to vary by factor level and I've attempted to incorporate both a mancova and anova approaches in the formula (sections 8.1 and 8.2) is this not the case? As I pointed out in section 1, all of the size variables are highly and significantly correlated - which is why I thought mancova would be the right approach. Additionally, I used anova (8.2) to see how each size variable is affected by data structure. Would you suggest a different approach?

How to implement an ancova approach with Procrustes anova?
model <- procD.lm(coords~size + region + pop * region/pop)
nested.update(model) = the * region/pop term from above

And repeat the above for each size variable?

In terms of the final analyses (section 9) I'm using the reduced PCA components of shape (from plotTangentSpace) in a multivariate multiple linear regression with PCA reduced frequency spectra (not reduced in geomorph). Here I call the lm function to test if shape affects frequency tuning - and it does. Is this not a sound approach? Is there a way to run this type of analysis using the full shape coordinates?  Currently my MMLA approach is:

fit <- lm(PCA reduced spectra ~ PCA reduced shape + region/pop

Once again thank you for your feedback - it's very much appreciated.

Cheers,
Jeremy

On Thu, May 24, 2018 at 10:30 PM, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> Jeremy,
>
>
>
> A few quick thoughts. First, if all variables are considered main effects, one should consider a factorial analysis in procD.lm: Y~pop + region + pop:region.  However, I suspect that your populations are nested within region, so a nested model is preferred. The help file of both procD.lm, advanced.procD.lm, and nested.update have more details on how to run this.
>
>
> Second you mentioned allometry. This too could be a factor in the model. That is actually important, because patterns of allometry may differ among factor levels; converting your problem to an ancova.
>
>
> Finally, at the end you mentioned running an analysis, reducing the data dimensions and running subsequent analyses on the reduced data. That is never a good idea: the algebra does not care about the dimensionality (at least as run in geomorph and the RRPP package). Take advantage of it and run it fully (note: reducing data one can both introduce patterns or miss patterns in the first few PC dimensions, as covariation of Y with X is not guaranteed to be in the first few PC dimensions of Y).

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Issue related to define.sliders
messages.body_plain:
Laurent,

this is not an issue of define.sliders, but rather a formatting problem in your original tps file, and specifically in the scale arguments of some specimens. For individuals 11 and 23 (codes Pygathrix_119648 Rhinopithecus_19502) the scale value in the tps file uses comma instead of point for the decimal mark. Because of that, geomorph does not read it in correctly, the coordinates cannot be scaled, and they are transformed to NAs, which is then causing the rest of your issues.

Your slider definition is OK, so the only thing you need to do is review your original file. I changed the commas to points manually and was able to run the rest of your script without problems, but probably you should review that file more generally, as the magnitude of those two scaling factors also looks off.

Hope this helps!

Antigoni

messages.subject: Re: QUESTION ABOUT GEOMORPH (procD.allometry
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicole,

some thoughts: your general approach is correct for analyzing your data.
However, the biological signal in your data seems to be "boarder-line"
in terms of whether or not you should consider different allometric
slopes for each group: the homogeneity of slopes test indicates
differences, but the effect is marginally not significant in your global
ANOVA table. For this reason, I recommend you run a pairwise comparison
of slopes using advanced.procD.lm(). This will allow you to evaluate the
strength and extension of slope divergence among your groups, and it
will help you decide whether your data justify using a model with
different slopes.

If you decide that it IS justified, interpretations should be made
focusing on the allometric slopes themselves, and not on the main
effects or two-way interactions, as is the case generally for more
complex interaction terms in ANOVAs.

As a side note, please use the geomorph googlegroup forum for future
communications and questions regarding geomorph:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/geomorph-r-package

This way users other than the geomorph developers can provide their
opinion and also benefit from this kind of questions. For reference, I
also recommend you search past conversations in the forum, as this kind
of topic has been treated before by other users.

Hope this helps!

Antigoni

For context, my previous colored plot script was as follows: I converted my excel tables into csv files and read them into R, then used prcomp to do PCA analyses. I then took the scores of the analyses (mydata$x), wrote them to csv files, and read those files into R again, assigning them to objects. I used RColorBrewer package next to make color palette vectors to assign colors to the species I labeled in my files, and also used pch to assign symbols for Male and Female specimens. Finally, I plotted, using the code below.

> plot(PCAnmdScores$PC1, PCAnmdScores$PC2, col=cols_speciesnmd, main="Principal Component Analysis", xlab = "PC1", ylab="PC2")

However, the plots I've gotten don't seem to be right. Maybe someone can help direct me to the right set of scores in my data that I'm supposed to be extracting? Or maybe I'm missing a step? > library(geomorph)

> plotTangentSpace(gpa.coords$coords)            (This is what I am trying to achieve a colored plot for)
> out.pca <- plotTangentSpace(gpa.coords$coords,label = TRUE)                  (Here I used the $scores of my out.pca and wrote them to a csv file, and later even tried a prcomp, but I think I was just totally on the wrong track here with this).

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

Though common in the literature, I would not reduce the dimensionality of the data via PCA. It can enhance or obscure pattern in the full (read: actual) dataspace.

Based on your question, you wish to know about spectral tuning vs. shape? In this case I would suggest two block partial least squares. This examines the covariation between two sets of variables. These are described in the various help files in geomorph.

Dean

Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Am I using the right approaches with this dataset?

Dean,

Thank you very much for your time, thoughtful comments and feedback. Actually my original approach included using procD.lm instead of advanced.procD.lm in order to look at factor interactions. But based on other conversations, I was persuaded to switch to advanced.procD.lm. Fortunately, whether I'm suing procD or advanced, all of the same trends appear from this dataset - so that's a plus. I will revisit using procD.lm incorporating nested.update for the factors.

Yes, allometry does seem to vary by factor level and I've attempted to incorporate both a mancova and anova approaches in the formula (sections 8.1 and 8.2) is this not the case? As I pointed out in section 1, all of the size variables are highly and significantly correlated - which is why I thought mancova would be the right approach. Additionally, I used anova (8.2) to see how each size variable is affected by data structure. Would you suggest a different approach?

How to implement an ancova approach with Procrustes anova?

model <- procD.lm(coords~size + region + pop * region/pop)

nested.update(model) = the * region/pop term from above

And repeat the above for each size variable?

In terms of the final analyses (section 9) I'm using the reduced PCA components of shape (from plotTangentSpace) in a multivariate multiple linear regression with PCA reduced frequency spectra (not reduced in geomorph). Here I call the lm function to test if shape affects frequency tuning - and it does. Is this not a sound approach? Is there a way to run this type of analysis using the full shape coordinates?  Currently my MMLA approach is:

fit <- lm(PCA reduced spectra ~ PCA reduced shape + region/pop

Once again thank you for your feedback - it's very much appreciated.

Cheers,

Jeremy

On Thu, May 24, 2018 at 10:30 PM, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> Jeremy,
>
>
>
> A few quick thoughts. First, if all variables are considered main effects, one should consider a factorial analysis in procD.lm: Y~pop + region + pop:region.  However, I suspect that your populations are nested within region, so a nested model is preferred. The help file of both procD.lm, advanced.procD.lm, and nested.update have more details on how to run this.
>
>
> Second you mentioned allometry. This too could be a factor in the model. That is actually important, because patterns of allometry may differ among factor levels; converting your problem to an ancova.
>
>
> Finally, at the end you mentioned running an analysis, reducing the data dimensions and running subsequent analyses on the reduced data. That is never a good idea: the algebra does not care about the dimensionality (at least as run in geomorph and the RRPP package). Take advantage of it and run it fully (note: reducing data one can both introduce patterns or miss patterns in the first few PC dimensions, as covariation of Y with X is not guaranteed to be in the first few PC dimensions of Y).
>
>
> Dean

> Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Am I using the right approaches with this dataset?

>
>
> Hi Geomorph Community,
>
>
>
> I have a complex dataset I'm working with and I would greatly appreciate some advice. In order to finalize my results I'd really like to know that my approach is actually appropriate to test my hypotheses. Here's a quick summary of the data that I have and my approach.
>
>
>
> I'm investigating how size and shape affect the tuning of ears in an insect. semilandmarks with curves were placed on 3D volumes of the hearing system of 48 individual animals. The 48 individuals are from 8 different populations (6/population) with uneven numbers of genders in each population. Although I'm not as concerned about differences in gender here. Also, the 8 populations separate out (nested) into a northern (4 populations) and southern region (4 populations). My hypotheses are: 1) Both size and shape affect tuning of the ear. 2) Shape (& size) differs by region and by population. I also have three different body size measurements: centroid size, prothorax width, and weight.
>
>
>
> My current approach:
> Investigation of size variables - e.g. distributions (weight needed to be log transformed as it differs significantly from a normal distribution), ANOVA (by gender (NS), region (highly significant for all three size variables) and by population (highly significant: post-hoc tests reveals 4 size classes for each size variable)), correlation matrix (all three size variables highly correlated)
> GPA of two sets of placed landmarks (to test for user error in placement)
> Test of user error <- proc.D.lm(coords ~ group) group contains set 1 and set 2 of placed landmarks - NS
> I am taking forward one set of the above GPA aligned coordinates in the below analyses
> Shape differs by population?
> advanced.procD.lm(coords~pop, ~1, groups = ~pop) - Highly significant with several significant pairwise comparisons
> Shape differs by region?
> advanced.procD.lm(coords~region, ~1, groups = ~ region) - significant but both f and z scores are low (2.23/2.1)
> Shape differs by gender?
> advanced.procD.lm(coords~gender, ~1, groups = ~gender) - NS
> Investigation of allometry without data structure
> Centroid size <- procD.lm(coords~Csize) - NS
> Prothorax width <- procD.lm(coords~prow) - Right at significance 0.05
> log(weight) <- procD.lm(coords~weight) - significant
> Investigation of allometry with data structure
> Are there differences in shape by population when accounting for body size?
> advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~Csize + prow + log(weight) + region * pop, groups = ~region*pop) - significant model with a few significant pairwise comparisons
> Are there differences in shape by population when accounting for separated out body size variables (this was done in order to get a better idea of how they interact with data structure alone)
> Centroid size <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~Csize + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with several significant pairwise comparisons
> Prothorax width <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~prow + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with a couple significant pairwise comparisons
> weight <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~log(weight) + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with several significant pairwise comparisons
> PCA reduced allometric shape and PCA reduced allometry free shape (from applying the residuals from the analyses in #7 on GPA consensus coordinates).
> PCA reduced shape is used in multivariate multiple linear regression analyses to address hypotheses 1.
>
> Does my above approach to address my second hypothesis seem reasonable? At present, these results support the conclusion that shape does differ by population, region and by size. Although pairwise comparisons suggest that not all populations differ significantly from each other (when accounting for all body size measurements or with them individually).
>
>
>
> Any insights and constructive comments are very welcomed and appreciated. As I've said, I am very interested in finalizing these results.
>
>
>
> Thank you in advance for your time - cheers,
>
> Jeremy
>
>

I also receive the error if I remove spectra from the analysis. Also, gdf = a geomorph data frame and all coords have a reference population (or site).

Thoughts?

Jeremy

That is never a good idea: the algebra does not care about the dimensionality (at least as run in geomorph and the RRPP package). messages.body_plain:
Hi Dean,

I spent the days  digging both in your just published paper (Adams & Collyer, 2018) and my data.

I have covariation between my behavioural factor (UBF) and diet so I used type II SS as you proposed and the results with the full model (shape ~ diet * UBF) and the results with the model only including the main effect of diet and the interaction of diet with the behavioural factor (shape ~ diet + diet:UBF) display similar stats. So that’s making more sense.

Also, I think that by visual inspection it can be argued I have some clade-group aggregation in my data (attached figure). I tested the PLS correlation between the phylogenetic covariation matrix and the design matrix by means of two block PLS and it is indeed strong and significant (rpls = 0.5-0.4, P = < .001) with both diet and UBF separately, although I am not sure if I did it completely right and I don’t really know how to get the whole design matrix, which is probably quite simple (code at the end of the email).

However, I checked Adams & Collyer, 2018 scripts in Dryad and it looks like you are not using any additional option other than SS.type = “II” to do the regressions/ANOVA using PGLS-t, does this mean the transformed  residuals are calculated by default when you include a phylogeny in geomorph 6.0.6?

Here my code for the intended PGLS linear model:

PGLS.coords_diet <- procD.pgls(coords ~ diet2*UBF.C, phy = phy, iter = 999, data = beak_data, print.progress = T, SS.type = "II")

Here for quantifying covariation between phylogeny and design matrix:

beak_data <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = beak_coords2, diet2 = diet2, MA = ant.MA2, BM = log.BM2, UBF.C = UBF1, phy = birdTree)

##Assess covariance between phylogenetic matrix and diet design matrix

phylo_m <- vcv.phylo(birdTree)

X <- model.matrix(~beak_data$diet2); rownames(X) <- row.names(beak_coords)

y<-two.b.pls(phylo_m, X, iter = 999)

Thank you very much for your kind attention,

Guille

Thus you are really doing Y~diet1+diet2+diet3… etc.  That is quite a large multivariate multiple PGLS regression.

> Second, you have a grouping factor, so phylogenetic anova.  BEFORE proceeding, be certain to download and install geomorph 3.0.6 from CRAN.  Yesterday we announced the version and the primary advance was a more appropriate permutation test for GLS models like phylogenetic anova (the corresponding paper is in press in Evolution).

>
>
> Third, the df do make sense in the full factorial. The df for an interaction in full factorial is dfA*dfB.  That is 10*4 = 40.
>
>
>
> As for the different ‘behavior’ (by this I think you meant significance), this one requires some more thinking about linear models. You are using type I SS, so each term in the 2 is being compared to a reduced model with one fewer term. The difference in how SS is partitioned in your two models relative to those reduced models will explain it.
>
>
>
> However, this may not be the most appropriate manner to evaluate your data if diet and UBF covary. If they do you may wish to use conditional (type II) SS.  See the example for phylogenetic MANCOVA in the evolution paper just mentioned (Adams and Collyer 2018. Evolution: early view on-line).

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

please have a better look at the help file of integration.test. The argument partition.gp <http://partition.gp> is used to subdivide a structure into two partitions for testing their integration, if that were the structure of your data (which it is not). If you want to examine how integration varies across groups, you will need more advanced methods, which could at present be partially implemented through the function compare.pls. For more details, please see Adams, D.C. and M.L. Collyer. 2016. On the comparison of the strength of morphological integration across morphometric datasets. Evolution. 70:2623-2631.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

Jeremy,

Two-block partial least squares evaluates the covariation between blocks: nothing more. It is not a linear model where one has other grouping factors. It flags an error because you are trying to do something with your data for which the method is not intended.

Dean

Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Am I using the right approaches with this dataset?

Hi Dean,

Once again thank you for your time and comments. Switching to the methods you suggest I would like to see how shape and population affects tuning but I've seem to run into an error that I'm not sure how to fix. Based on the help files in geomorph I have settled on using the function 'integration.test'. Here's how I've run the tests.

PLS1 <- integration.test(gdf$coords, spectra, iter = 999, seed = NULL, print.progress = TRUE)

In this configuration I get a significant result.

PLS2 <- integration.test(gdf$coords, spectra,  partition.gp <http://partition.gp> = gdf$site, iter = 999, seed = NUMM, print.progress = TRUE)

here I receive an error: Error in integration.test(gdf$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp> = gdf$site, iter = Reps, : Not all landmarks are assigned to a partition.

I also receive the error if I remove spectra from the analysis. Also, gdf = a geomorph data frame and all coords have a reference population (or site).

Thoughts?

Thanks - Cheers,

Jeremy

But based on other conversations, I was persuaded to switch to advanced.procD.lm. Fortunately, whether I'm suing procD or advanced, all of the same trends appear from this dataset - so that's a plus. I will revisit using procD.lm incorporating nested.update for the factors.
>
>
>
> Yes, allometry does seem to vary by factor level and I've attempted to incorporate both a mancova and anova approaches in the formula (sections 8.1 and 8.2) is this not the case? As I pointed out in section 1, all of the size variables are highly and significantly correlated - which is why I thought mancova would be the right approach. Here I call the lm function to test if shape affects frequency tuning - and it does. Is this not a sound approach? Is there a way to run this type of analysis using the full shape coordinates? >

> On Thu, May 24, 2018 at 10:30 PM, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> > A few quick thoughts. First, if all variables are considered main effects, one should consider a factorial analysis in procD.lm: Y~pop + region + pop:region.  However, I suspect that your populations are nested within region, so a nested model is preferred. The help file of both procD.lm, advanced.procD.lm, and nested.update have more details on how to run this.
> >
> >
> > Second you mentioned allometry. This too could be a factor in the model. That is actually important, because patterns of allometry may differ among factor levels; converting your problem to an ancova.
> >
> >
> > Finally, at the end you mentioned running an analysis, reducing the data dimensions and running subsequent analyses on the reduced data. That is never a good idea: the algebra does not care about the dimensionality (at least as run in geomorph and the RRPP package). Take advantage of it and run it fully (note: reducing data one can both introduce patterns or miss patterns in the first few PC dimensions, as covariation of Y with X is not guaranteed to be in the first few PC dimensions of Y).

> >
> > I'm investigating how size and shape affect the tuning of ears in an insect. semilandmarks with curves were placed on 3D volumes of the hearing system of 48 individual animals. The 48 individuals are from 8 different populations (6/population) with uneven numbers of genders in each population. Although I'm not as concerned about differences in gender here. Also, the 8 populations separate out (nested) into a northern (4 populations) and southern region (4 populations). My hypotheses are: 1) Both size and shape affect tuning of the ear. 2) Shape (& size) differs by region and by population. I also have three different body size measurements: centroid size, prothorax width, and weight.
> >
> >
> >
> > My current approach:
> > Investigation of size variables - e.g. distributions (weight needed to be log transformed as it differs significantly from a normal distribution), ANOVA (by gender (NS), region (highly significant for all three size variables) and by population (highly significant: post-hoc tests reveals 4 size classes for each size variable)), correlation matrix (all three size variables highly correlated)
> > GPA of two sets of placed landmarks (to test for user error in placement)
> > Test of user error <- proc.D.lm(coords ~ group) group contains set 1 and set 2 of placed landmarks - NS
> > I am taking forward one set of the above GPA aligned coordinates in the below analyses
> > Shape differs by population?

> > Shape differs by region?
> > advanced.procD.lm(coords~region, ~1, groups = ~ region) - significant but both f and z scores are low (2.23/2.1)
> > Shape differs by gender?

> > Investigation of allometry without data structure
> > Centroid size <- procD.lm(coords~Csize) - NS
> > Prothorax width <- procD.lm(coords~prow) - Right at significance 0.05
> > log(weight) <- procD.lm(coords~weight) - significant
> > Investigation of allometry with data structure
> > Are there differences in shape by population when accounting for body size?
> > advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~Csize + prow + log(weight) + region * pop, groups = ~region*pop) - significant model with a few significant pairwise comparisons
> > Are there differences in shape by population when accounting for separated out body size variables (this was done in order to get a better idea of how they interact with data structure alone)
> > Centroid size <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~Csize + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with several significant pairwise comparisons
> > Prothorax width <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~prow + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with a couple significant pairwise comparisons
> > weight <- advanced.procD.lm(coords~1, ~log(weight) + region * pop, groups = ~ region * pop) - significant model with several significant pairwise comparisons
> > PCA reduced allometric shape and PCA reduced allometry free shape (from applying the residuals from the analyses in #7 on GPA consensus coordinates).
> > PCA reduced shape is used in multivariate multiple linear regression analyses to address hypotheses 1.
> >
> > Does my above approach to address my second hypothesis seem reasonable? At present, these results support the conclusion that shape does differ by population, region and by size. Although pairwise comparisons suggest that not all populations differ significantly from each other (when accounting for all body size measurements or with them individually).
> >
> >
> >
> > Any insights and constructive comments are very welcomed and appreciated. As I've said, I am very interested in finalizing these results.
> >
> >
> >
> > Thank you in advance for your time - cheers,
> >
> > Jeremy

Guille,

>From what you described, you definitely have group * phylogeny covariation. So please be sure to use the latest version of geomorph which uses RRPP to randomize phylogenetically-transformed residuals.

As for the factorial analysis, yes, we did not include the type II SS analysis in the supplemental material, as this is specific to one’s data and requires investigation first (as we clearly describe in the paper). We did not want folks to just ‘follow the script’ if it were provided. However, using geomorph 3.0.6, any type of SS being used are properly transformed by the phylogeny during the analysis.

Best,

Dean

Hi Dean,

I spent the days  digging both in your just published paper (Adams & Collyer, 2018) and my data.

I have covariation between my behavioural factor (UBF) and diet so I used type II SS as you proposed and the results with the full model (shape ~ diet * UBF) and the results with the model only including the main effect of diet and the interaction of diet with the behavioural factor (shape ~ diet + diet:UBF) display similar stats. So that’s making more sense.

Also, I think that by visual inspection it can be argued I have some clade-group aggregation in my data (attached figure). I tested the PLS correlation between the phylogenetic covariation matrix and the design matrix by means of two block PLS and it is indeed strong and significant (rpls = 0.5-0.4, P = < .001) with both diet and UBF separately, although I am not sure if I did it completely right and I don’t really know how to get the whole design matrix, which is probably quite simple (code at the end of the email).

However, I checked Adams & Collyer, 2018 scripts in Dryad and it looks like you are not using any additional option other than SS.type = “II” to do the regressions/ANOVA using PGLS-t, does this mean the transformed  residuals are calculated by default when you include a phylogeny in geomorph 6.0.6?

Here my code for the intended PGLS linear model:

PGLS.coords_diet <- procD.pgls(coords ~ diet2*UBF.C, phy = phy, iter = 999, data = beak_data, print.progress = T, SS.type = "II")

Here for quantifying covariation between phylogeny and design matrix:

beak_data <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = beak_coords2, diet2 = diet2, MA = ant.MA2, BM = log.BM2, UBF.C = UBF1, phy = birdTree)

##Assess covariance between phylogenetic matrix and diet design matrix

phylo_m <- vcv.phylo(birdTree)

X <- model.matrix(~beak_data$diet2); rownames(X) <- row.names(beak_coords)

y<-two.b.pls(phylo_m, X, iter = 999)

Thank you very much for your kind attention,

Guille

Thus you are really doing Y~diet1+diet2+diet3… etc.  That is quite a large multivariate multiple PGLS regression.
>
>
>
> Second, you have a grouping factor, so phylogenetic anova.  BEFORE proceeding, be certain to download and install geomorph 3.0.6 from CRAN.  Yesterday we announced the version and the primary advance was a more appropriate permutation test for GLS models like phylogenetic anova (the corresponding paper is in press in Evolution).

>
>
> Third, the df do make sense in the full factorial. The df for an interaction in full factorial is dfA*dfB.  That is 10*4 = 40.
>
>
>
> As for the different ‘behavior’ (by this I think you meant significance), this one requires some more thinking about linear models. You are using type I SS, so each term in the 2 is being compared to a reduced model with one fewer term. The difference in how SS is partitioned in your two models relative to those reduced models will explain it.
>
>
>
> However, this may not be the most appropriate manner to evaluate your data if diet and UBF covary. If they do you may wish to use conditional (type II) SS.  See the example for phylogenetic MANCOVA in the evolution paper just mentioned (Adams and Collyer 2018. Evolution: early view on-line).
